dedupe_keys.name: dhaka robust optimisation of ambulance outpost locations and motorcycle ambulances

description: This case study optimises where to base emergency response vehicles and how to route them in Dhaka, Bangladesh, a city with little emergency medical transport. Justin Boutilier and Timothy Chan of the University of Toronto travelled to Dhaka to collect two field datasets, which they used to build machine learning methods that estimate demand for emergency medical services and predict travel times between any two points on the road network by time of day and day of week. They combined these with a robust optimisation model for vehicle location and routing that allows for uncertain travel times and demand. The article was published in Operations Research in 2020, and an author version is free to read online on arXiv. Coverage is one megacity. Caveats: the field datasets are not stated to be public, and the results depend on model assumptions about demand. The authors show that outpost locations optimised for weekday rush hour perform well at all times; that relocating a few outposts gives large improvements in response times, and current performance could be matched with 30 percent of the resources; and that a fleet of small motorcycle ambulances could greatly outperform traditional vans, capturing three times more demand. Simulation uses: demand and travel time methods and policy results for ambulance planning in low- and middle-income cities. Related records: the Liberia national EMS study (case_study-liberia-national-ems-first-22-months) and the Iceland helicopter base study (case_study-iceland-helicopter-ambulance-base-location) cover other settings.
